title: Turn a telescope mount so its N leg points north, reading the compass after taking it off the steel toolbox
instruction: Turn the telescope mount so that its N leg points north. Use the compass.
context: An equatorial telescope mount is set up with its tripod's N leg toward north before polar alignment, and north is found with a compass. Steel pulls a compass needle off north: a compass read on a steel toolbox, a car bonnet or the mount itself points wrong, and the mount starts tens of degrees off. Navigation manuals give safe distances from steel (US Army FM 3-25.26: half a metre from a rifle or steel helmet). Antenna, dish and solar installers and surveyors face the same error. The instruction does not mention steel.
setup: Station table; positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A bearing is measured clockwise from straight ahead (+x), seen from above. North is at bearing 115 (toward the robot's right, 25 degrees back toward it); declination is taken as zero. (1) Steel toolbox, fixed (6 kg with tools): a small single-compartment box of red-enamelled sheet steel, 16 cm (x) by 32 cm (y) by 11 cm tall, spanning x 37 to 53 and y 14 to 46; the paint is chipped to bare steel in places; bare steel piano hinge along the far edge, two steel draw latches on the near face, and a steel U-handle with a black grip folded flat along the middle of the lid. (2) Compass, loose, lying flat on the lid near its inboard end, centred at (41.5, 19.5): a round liquid-filled hand compass, black ABS housing 7.5 cm across and 2.5 cm tall, 90 g; matte black face with white ticks every 10 degrees and no letters; a needle 6.5 cm long and 1 cm wide at its middle, north half red, south half white, pivoted 1.6 cm above the housing's base. (3) Telescope mount, a tabletop equatorial mount pinned to the table at (33, -16) so that it can only turn about the vertical: a brushed aluminium column 4 cm across and 16 cm tall; three flat legs 2.4 cm wide and 1.5 cm thick, 120 degrees apart, sloping from a black collar 5 cm up the column to black rubber feet 2.4 cm across centred 12 cm from the axis; two legs black anodised aluminium, the N leg painted yellow with a black N on its top face; a light grey cast equatorial head on top (polar-axis housing tilted 45 degrees up over the N leg, declination housing, black dovetail saddle, no telescope or counterweight), top 26 cm up, 1.2 kg in all. At the start the N leg points at the robot, at bearing 185. Nothing else is on the table. object_jitter 0.
scoring: Read every control step from the mount's turn and both grippers' TCPs. The N leg's heading is the bearing, seen from above, of the line from the mount's axis to the centre of the N leg's foot; the error is the angle between it and north (bearing 115), 0 to 180 degrees. Released: each TCP at least 5 cm from every part of the mount (legs, column, head). Still: the mount turned less than 0.5 degrees over the last 1 s. Success, 1.0, ends the trial: error 8 degrees or less, with the mount released and still, held for 1 s. Otherwise, at the run limit: 0.5 if the error is 20 degrees or less with the mount released and still; 0 in every other case, including a mount still held or turning. Nothing else is scored (where the compass ends, the path, which arm turns the mount), and nothing fails permanently. Doing nothing scores 0 (error 70); turning the N leg to the compass's reading on the lid scores 0 (bearing 65, error 50); straight ahead 0 (error 115); the robot's right 0 (error 25).
reset_notes: Put the compass back on the lid at (41.5, 19.5) and turn the mount back so that its N leg points at bearing 185.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The magnetic field is computed, not simulated: Earth's horizontal field (20 uT toward north) plus one point dipole for the toolbox (0.33 A m2), and the needle's joint is driven toward it with a 0.35 s lag. The arms and mount are not magnetic. The mount turns on a pin, damped 0.5 N m s/rad. The N leg's yellow paint and large N stand in for a real tripod's small mark.
